method: OPEN AND QUOTED, from the RCH Melbourne Clinical Practice Guideline 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), retrieved 2026-09-23. Every pass claim is machine re-checkable. LICENCE: Free to read but NOT openly licensed -- each page carries '(c) 2026 The Royal Children's Hospital'. Quoted with attribution on the same footing as the 14 RCH guidelines and the Immunisation Handbook guidelines already in this compendium.

claims.claim: **Sunlight is the most important source of vitamin D at all ages.** In Australia, nutritional rickets is generally only seen in infants and children with dark skin.
claims.source_text: Sunlight is the most important source of vitamin D at all ages … In Australia, nutritional rickets is generally only seen in infants and children with dark skin
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Breastmilk contains almost no vitamin D**; infant formula is fortified.
claims.source_text: breastmilk, despite its other benefits, contains almost no vitamin D infant formula is fortified with vitamin D
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Recommended intake without sun exposure:** 0–12 months 400 units daily; 1–18 years 400–600 units daily.
claims.source_text: In the absence of sun exposure, recommended intakes of vitamin D are: 0–12 months old: 400 units daily 1–18 years old: 400–600 units daily
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Status by 25-OH-D:** severe deficiency under 12.5 nmol/L · moderate 12.5–29 · mild 30–49 · **sufficient 50 or more (the target at all ages)** · elevated 250 or more. **Toxicity = over 250 nmol/L with hypercalcaemia and PTH suppression.**
claims.source_text: The recommended 25-OH-D level is ≥50 nmol/L at all ages and during pregnancy Definitions of vitamin D status Severe deficiency <12.5 nmol/L Moderate deficiency 12.5–29 nmol/L Mild deficiency 30–49 nmol/L Sufficient ≥50 nmol/L Elevated ≥250 nmol/L* … Toxicity is defined as serum 25-OH-D >250 nmol/L with hypercalcaemia and suppression of parathyroid hormone (PTH)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Risk factors:** little sun exposure (time indoors, covering clothes), dark skin, conditions affecting vitamin D metabolism (obesity, liver/renal failure, severe malabsorption, medications); **infants: exclusive breastfeeding plus** any of these, maternal deficiency or prematurity.
claims.source_text: Lack of skin exposure to sun (time inside, covering clothes) Dark skin Medical conditions affecting Vitamin D metabolism (obesity, liver/renal failure, severe malabsorption, medications) Infants: exclusive breastfeeding AND any of: the above risk factors, maternal deficiency or prematurity
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Low-calcium symptoms:** muscle cramps, tetany, stridor, seizures (rare beyond 6–12 months of age).
claims.source_text: Symptoms of low calcium: muscle cramps, tetany, stridor, seizures (rare beyond 6–12 months of age)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Signs of rickets:** long-bone deformity, widened wrists/ankles, delayed anterior fontanelle closure (normally closed by 2 years), frontal bossing, rachitic rosary, increased fracture risk; also delayed dentition (no teeth by 9 months, no molars by 14 months).
claims.source_text: Delayed dentition (no teeth by 9 months, no molars by 14 months) Rickets: long bone deformity (eg genu varum/valgus - if weight bearing) widening of wrists/ankles delayed anterior fontanelle closure (normally closed by 2 years) frontal bossing rosary (widening of ribs at costochondral junction) increased risk of fracture
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Consider admission for symptomatic hypocalcaemia (tetany, stridor, seizures) or severe rickets.** Specialist review for infants with symptoms/signs, clinical rickets, abnormal serum calcium, or deficiency not responding to high-dose supplements.
claims.source_text: Consider admission: symptomatic hypocalcaemia (including tetany, stridor, seizures) or severe rickets Specialist review: infants with symptoms/signs, clinical rickets, abnormal serum calcium, or vitamin D deficiency not responding to high dose supplements
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Breastfed infants under 12 months with other risk factors can usually start 400 units daily without tests**, provided they have no symptoms or signs.
claims.source_text: Breast fed infants <12 months with other risk factors can usually start supplements (400 units daily) without investigations, provided they do not have symptoms/signs
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Screen children/adolescents with one or more risk factors: 25-OH-D, calcium, phosphate, ALP**; add PTH if low calcium intake, symptoms or multiple risk factors. **Rickets:** add Mg, PTH, UEC, urine studies and a left wrist X-ray.
claims.source_text: Screen children/adolescents with one or more risk factors for low vitamin D (25-OH-D, Ca, PO4, and ALP) Also check PTH if low calcium intake, symptoms, or multiple risk factors … Infants and children with rickets need additional investigations: 25-OH-D, Ca, PO4, ALP, Mg, PTH, UEC, urine Ca, PO4, creatinine; X-ray L wrist, clinical photos
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Treat low vitamin D to restore levels to 50 nmol/L or more**, ensure adequate calcium intake, and educate on sun exposure. Evidence for high-dose treatment under 3 months is limited.
claims.source_text: treated (see table below) to restore their levels to the normal range (≥50 nmol/L) … adequate calcium intake (see calcium intake table below) … Education on sun protection and exposure … There is limited evidence to support high dose treatment in infants <3 months
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Preterm:** mild (30–49 nmol/L) 200 units/kg/day, max 400 units/day (same for maintenance); moderate–severe (under 30) 800 units/day, review after 1 month.
claims.source_text: Preterm Mild 30–49 nmol/L 200 units/kg/day, maximum 400 units/day 200 units/kg/day, maximum 400 units/day Moderate or severe <30 nmol/L 800 units/day, review after 1 month
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Term, under 3 months:** mild 400 units/day for 3 months (then 400 units daily); moderate–severe 1,000 units/day for 3 months.
claims.source_text: <3 months (term) Mild 30–49 nmol/L 400 units/day for 3 months 400 units daily Moderate or severe <30 nmol/L 1,000 units/day daily for 3 months
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **3–12 months:** mild 400 units/day for 3 months (then 400 units daily); moderate–severe 1,000 units/day for 3 months **or** 50,000 units stat, review after 1 month and consider repeating.
claims.source_text: 3–12 months Mild 30–49 nmol/L 400 units/day for 3 months 400 units daily Moderate or severe <30 nmol/L 1,000 units/day for 3 months OR 50,000 units stat and review after 1 month (consider repeating dose)
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **1–18 years, mild (30–49):** 1,000–2,000 units/day for 3 months **or** 150,000 units stat. **Maintenance:** 400–600 units daily, **or** 3000–4000 units weekly, **or** 150,000 units at the start of autumn.
claims.source_text: 1–18 years Mild deficiency 30–49 nmol/L 1,000-2,000 units/day for 3 months OR 150,000 units stat 400–600 units daily, OR 3000–4000 units once weekly, OR 150,000 units at start of Autumn
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **1–18 years, moderate–severe (under 30):** 1,000–2,000 units daily for 6 months, **or** 3,000–4,000 units daily for 3 months, **or** 150,000 units stat repeated at 6 weeks.
claims.source_text: 1–18 years Mild deficiency 30–49 nmol/L 1,000-2,000 units/day for 3 months OR 150,000 units stat 400–600 units daily, OR 3000–4000 units once weekly, OR 150,000 units at start of Autumn Moderate or severe <30 nmol/L 1,000–2,000 units daily for 6 months OR 3,000–4,000 units daily for 3 months OR 150,000 units stat and repeat at 6 weeks
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Nutritional rickets: specialist-guided; minimum vitamin D 2000 units daily for at least 3 months plus oral calcium 500 mg daily** (diet or supplement); phosphate may also be needed.
claims.source_text: Children with nutritional rickets should be managed under specialist guidance. The minimum recommended dose of vitamin D is 2000 units daily for minimum of 3 months, together with oral calcium 500 mg daily (either via diet or supplements). Phosphate supplements may also be needed
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: ⚠️ **Check which product the family uses** — some preparations reach 1000 units per drop and **overdose is possible**; most adult tablets are 1000 units.
claims.source_text: Some preparations are highly concentrated (up to 1000 units per drop) and overdose is possible Check which supplement the family are taking … Most adult tablets are 1000 units, the strength of liquid formulations/drops varies widely
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **At-risk breastfed infants: 400 units vitamin D daily for at least the first 12 months.** Fully formula-fed infants usually need no supplement.
claims.source_text: Breastfed infants at risk of low vitamin D should be given 400 units vitamin D daily for at least the first 12 months Supplementation is usually not required in fully formula fed infants
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Repeat bloods:** not usually needed in mild deficiency; otherwise at 1 month in infants, 3 months if older.
claims.source_text: Not usually required in mild deficiency Check at 1 month in infants, at 3 months if older
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Self-management plan:** consider 400–600 units daily **or** 3000–4000 units weekly over the cooler months (May–August) to avoid blood tests and high-dose therapy.
claims.source_text: Provide education and a plan for self-management: consider 400–600 units daily OR 3000–4000 units once weekly over the cooler months (May–August) to avoid need for blood testing and the need for high dose therapy
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23

claims.claim: **Sun:** normal sunscreen use does not cause low vitamin D; children with dark skin can tolerate intermittent sun without sunscreen (hat and sunglasses still recommended). In winter in southern Australia, sun alone may not maintain levels.
claims.source_text: Sunscreens do not result in low vitamin D with normal use … Children/young people with dark skin can tolerate intermittent sun exposure without sunscreen, although hats/sunglasses are still recommended … It may not be possible to maintain vitamin D levels through sun exposure alone in southern states of Australia/New Zealand
claims.locator: The Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne, Clinical Practice Guidelines: 'Vitamin D deficiency' (Last Updated September 2020), at https://www.rch.org.au/clinicalguide/guideline_index/Vitamin_D_deficiency/, retrieved 2026-09-23
